The Battle of Five Armies was a major conflict fought on and near the Lonely Mountain between the Goblins and Wargs of the Misty Mountains and Grey Mountains on one side, and the Lake-men, Elves, and Dwarves on the other [2]. According to the context, this battle occurred after forces had been gathering in the mountains, with "a vast host" assembled at Gundabad of the North, their capital, ready to sweep down upon the South [2].

The battle resulted in significant casualties among the defenders. In one adaptation, only seven of the original thirteen members of Thorin's company survived the battle, with Thorin himself mortally wounded [4]. Bombur was among those killed—in the 1977 animated version, he died after delivering news of the victory to Bilbo with his last words being "We won" [3][4].

In Peter Jackson's film adaptation, the battle was presented as a five-way conflict between the Dwarves of Erebor, Elves of Mirkwood, and Lake-men (aided by Gandalf, Bilbo, Beorn, and the Great Eagles) against two separate Orc armies from Dol Guldur and Gundabad [4].
reference: The Battle of Five Armies was fought at the Lonely Mountain (Erebor) after Smaug's death. In Tolkien's Middle-earth, mithril is extremely rare by the end of the Third Age, as it was now found only in Khazad-dûm. Once the Balrog destroyed Khazad-dûm, the kingdom of the Dwarves in Moria, the only source of new mithril ore was cut off. Before Moria was abandoned by the Dwarves, while it was still being actively mined, mithril was worth ten times its weight in gold. After the Dwarves abandoned Moria and production of new mithril stopped entirely, it became priceless.
Tolkien hints that mithril was found in the lost island kingdom of Númenor and the inaccessible continent of Aman.", '=== The mithril-coat ===
The principal item made of mithril in the works of Tolkien is the "small coat of mail" that Thorin Oakenshield gave to Bilbo Baggins after it had been retrieved from the hoard of Smaug the dragon. Gandalf stated that the value of this mithril-coat was "greater than the value of the whole Shire and everything in it". The mail-shirt was first described in The Hobbit in 1937, but without any mention of mithril. Tolkien first described the shirt as being made of mithril in The Lord of the Rings in 1954, and it was retrospectively mentioned in the third, revised edition of The Hobbit in 1966. In the first 1937 edition, the mail shirt given to Bilbo Baggins is described as being made of "silvered steel".', 'Nenya, the Ring of Power wielded by Galadriel, was made of mithril.
The guards of the citadel of Minas Tirith wore helmets of mithril, "heirlooms from the glory of old days". They were the only soldiers in Gondor who still bore the emblems of the lost kings during the days of the stewards.
As Aragorn's ships sailed up the Anduin to relieve the besieged Minas Tirith during the Battle of the Pelennor Fields, the standard flying on his ship showed a crown made of mithril and gold.
After Gimli became lord of Aglarond, he and his Dwarves forged great gates of mithril and steel to replace the gates of Minas Tirith, which had been broken by the Witch-king of Angmar.', 'The Tolkien critic Paul Kocher interprets the Dwarves' intense secrecy around mithril and their devotion to artistry in metal and stone as "a sublimation of their sexual frustration", given that they have very few dwarf-women and love beauty with a "jealous possessiveness", or (quoting Tolkien) "being engrossed in their crafts".
The name "mithril" (also spelt mith, mithral, or mythril) is used in multiple fictional contexts influenced by Tolkien. For example, the Final Fantasy game series, begun in 1987, involves dwarves and mithril.']
response:
Based on the provided context, mithril is an extremely rare and valuable metal in Tolkien's Middle-earth [1].

By the end of the Third Age, mithril was found only in Khazad-dûm (Moria), and once the Balrog destroyed this dwarven kingdom, the only source of new mithril ore was cut off [1]. When Moria was still being actively mined, mithril was worth ten times its weight in gold, but after the Dwarves abandoned it and production stopped, it became priceless [1]. Tolkien also hints that mithril existed in Númenor and Aman [1].

The most famous mithril item is the "small coat of mail" that Thorin Oakenshield gave to Bilbo Baggins, which Gandalf said was "greater than the value of the whole Shire and everything in it" [2]. Other notable mithril objects include Galadriel's Ring of Power, Nenya [3], the helmets worn by guards of Minas Tirith's citadel [3], and the great gates of Minas Tirith forged by Gimli and his Dwarves after the War of the Ring [3].
reference: Mithril is a fictional silver-like metal in Tolkien's Middle-earth, stronger and lighter than steel. It was found and mined by the Dwarves in Moria (Khazad-dûm). It was extremely valuable; Bilbo's mithril mail shirt, later worn by Frodo, is a notable example of its use.

=== Tom Bombadil ===

Tom Bombadil does not belong to any of the peoples of Middle-earth; Tolkien calls him the spirit of the countryside. Unlike the other races, he is seemingly unaffected by the One Ring and appears to have existed before the Children of Ilúvatar (Elves and Men). As to the nature of Bombadil, Tolkien himself said that some things should remain mysterious in any mythology, "especially if an explanation actually exists." Tom is also known as "The First", "Master Tom", "Old Tom", "Iarwain Ben-adar" (a Sindarin name meaning "The Oldest without a father"). The Noldor call him "Orald" meaning "Very Old", Dwarves call him "Forn" (meaning: The Ancient).', 'Tolkien commented further that "even in a mythical Age there must be some enigmas, as there always are. Tom Bombadil is one (intentionally)". In a letter to Stanley Unwin, Tolkien called Tom Bombadil the spirit of the vanishing landscapes of Oxfordshire and Berkshire. However, this 1937 letter was in reference to works which pre-dated the writing of The Lord of the Rings.', 'Tolkien stated that he invented Tom Bombadil in memory of his children's Dutch doll. His Bombadil poems far pre-date the writing of The Lord of the Rings, into which Tolkien introduced Tom Bombadil from the earliest drafts. In response to a letter, Tolkien described Tom in The Lord of the Rings as "just an invention" and "not an important person – to the narrative", even if "he represents something that I feel important, though I would not be prepared to analyse the feeling precisely. I would not, however, have left him in, if he did not have some kind of function." Specifically, Tolkien connected Tom in the letter to a renunciation of control, "a delight in things for themselves without reference to yourself," "Botany and Zoology (as sciences) and Poetry"']
response:
Tom Bombadil is a unique and deliberately enigmatic figure in Tolkien's Middle-earth. He does not belong to any of the peoples of Middle-earth; Tolkien calls him "the spirit of the countryside" [2]. Unlike other races, he is seemingly unaffected by the One Ring and appears to have existed before the Elves and Men [2]. He is known by various names: "The First," "Master Tom," "Old Tom," "Iarwain Ben-adar" (Sindarin for "The Oldest without a father"), "Orald" among the Noldor (meaning "Very Old"), and "Forn" among the Dwarves (meaning "The Ancient") [2].

Tolkien intentionally left Tom's nature mysterious, stating that "even in a mythical Age there must be some enigmas" and that Tom Bombadil is "one (intentionally)" [3]. The character was invented in memory of Tolkien's children's Dutch doll [4]. While Tolkien described Tom as "not an important person – to the narrative," he acknowledged that Tom "represents something that I feel important," connecting him to "a renunciation of control, a delight in things for themselves without reference to yourself," and to "Botany and Zoology (as sciences) and Poetry" [4].
reference: Tom Bombadil is an enigmatic character in The Lord of the Rings who lives in the Old Forest with his wife Goldberry. He is unaffected by the One Ring: it does not turn him invisible and has no power over him. Tolkien deliberately left his true nature and origin unexplained.
